title: Continuous frames identify coefficient sheaves and their scalar extension
statement:
Let $K$ be a field with a topology making its field operations continuous, and let $A\subseteq K$ be a subring with the subspace topology. Let $r\geq0$ and $L\subseteq K^r$ be an $A$-submodule, with the subspace topology from the product topology. Suppose $b_1,\ldots,b_r\in L$ are an $A$-basis of $L$ and a $K$-basis of $K^r$, and that $\beta:A^r\to L$, $(a_i)\mapsto\sum_i a_i b_i$, is a homeomorphism. Let $S$ be any scheme [def-pc-scheme], with its small pro-étale site [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site]. For a topological ring $T$, put $T_S(U)=C(|U|,T)$ with pointwise operations and precomposition restrictions, as in [def-weil-pbc-lisse-lattice-coefficients]. Define $F_L(U)=C(|U|,L)$ with pointwise $A_S(U)$-action and the same restrictions. Then $A_S,K_S$ are sheaves of rings and $F_L$ is a sheaf of $A_S$-modules [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. The maps
$$\phi_U:A_S(U)^r\xrightarrow{\sim}F_L(U),\qquad (a_i)\mapsto\bigl(x\mapsto\sum_i a_i(x)b_i\bigr),$$
with inverse $f\mapsto(x\mapsto(\beta^{-1}(f(x)))_i)_i$, are $A_S(U)$-linear isomorphisms commuting with every restriction. In particular $F_L\cong A_S^r$ as module sheaves. The actual inclusion $\iota:F_L\hookrightarrow K_S^r$ is postcomposition with $L\subseteq K^r$. For every $U$, its scalar-extension map
$$\mu_U:K_S(U)\otimes_{A_S(U)}F_L(U)\xrightarrow{\sim}C(|U|,K^r),\qquad a\otimes f\mapsto\bigl(x\mapsto a(x)f(x)\bigr)$$
is a $K_S(U)$-linear isomorphism. If $B\in\operatorname{GL}_r(K)$ has columns $b_i$ and $\underline b_i$ denotes the constant $L$-valued section, its inverse sends $g$ to $\sum_i (B^{-1}g)_i\otimes\underline b_i$. The maps $\mu_U$ and their inverses commute with every restriction. Under $\phi_U$ and the identification $a\otimes(a_i)_i\mapsto(aa_i)_i$, the map $\mu_U$ is multiplication by the constant matrix $B$. Thus the presheaf tensor product is already a sheaf, and the morphism $K_S\otimes_{A_S}F_L\to K_S^r$ induced by $\iota$ is an isomorphism for the sheaf tensor product [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product]. All assertions include $r=0$.

proof.text: Addition and negation on $A$, $K$ and $L$ are continuous: for $A$ and $L$ these are restrictions of the operations on $K$ and $K^r$ with their subspace topologies. The map $A\times L\to L$, $(a,v)\mapsto av$, is continuous for the same reason, coordinate by coordinate. Thus pointwise multiplication, addition and scalar multiplication preserve continuous maps. Precomposition preserves these operations, since $(af)\circ h=(a\circ h)(f\circ h)$. These are the presheaf ring and module structures specified in [def-weil-pbc-lisse-lattice-coefficients] and [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category].

proof.text: Apply [lem-cbc-continuous-functions-fpqc-sheaf] to the additive topological groups $A$, $K$ and $L$. It gives the sheaf condition for continuous functions on every fpqc cover. Every small pro-étale covering is such a cover by [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site], so the same unique gluing works on $S_{\mathrm{proét}}$. The pointwise operations of step 1 make $A_S,K_S$ sheaves of rings, and $F_L$ a sheaf of $A_S$-modules by [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]: the module laws hold at each point and the restrictions are semilinear. No separation hypothesis on the topological groups is needed.

proof.text: For $Z=|U|$, a tuple $(a_i)$ of continuous $A$-valued functions defines a continuous map $Z\to A^r$, since each coordinate is continuous. Compose with the given homeomorphism $\beta$ to obtain $\phi_U((a_i))$. Conversely the $i$th coordinate of $\beta^{-1}\circ f$ is continuous. The identities $\beta^{-1}\beta=1$ and $\beta\beta^{-1}=1$ prove the two inverse identities. The $A$-linearity of $\beta$ implies $\phi_U(c(a_i))=c\phi_U((a_i))$ pointwise, and likewise additivity. For every arrow $h:V\to U$, both $\beta\circ(a_i)\circ|h|$ and $\beta^{-1}\circ f\circ|h|$ are the corresponding restricted formulas. The inverses therefore define an isomorphism $A_S^r\cong F_L$ of module sheaves.

proof.text: The inclusion $L\hookrightarrow K^r$ is continuous and injective. Postcomposing sections gives the stated injective map into $C(|U|,K^r)$; coordinate projections identify this last module with $K_S(U)^r$, with inverse $(g_i)\mapsto(x\mapsto(g_i(x))_i)$. These maps commute with restrictions and are linear. Let $B$ have columns $b_i$. The hypothesis that these columns are a $K$-basis gives its inverse matrix $B^{-1}$. The maps $v\mapsto Bv$ and $v\mapsto B^{-1}v$ on $K^r$ are continuous: each coordinate is a finite sum of constant multiples of coordinates. In the frame of step 3, the actual inclusion sends $(a_i)$ to $B(a_i)$.

source.place: Pushing down by the trace: finite free constant lattice spanning the ambient vector space; explicit coordinate argument

proof.text: Write $R=A_S(U)$ and $T=K_S(U)$. The formula $(a,f)\mapsto(x\mapsto a(x)f(x))$ has continuous values, is additive in both arguments and is $R$-balanced, because $(ac)f=a(cf)$ pointwise for $c\in R$. Hence it induces the stated $T$-linear map $\mu_U:T\otimes_R F_L(U)\to C(|U|,K^r)$. Define $\psi_U(g)=\sum_i(B^{-1}g)_i\otimes\underline b_i$. Its coefficient functions are continuous by step 4, and the formula is $T$-linear. First $\mu_U\psi_U(g)=B(B^{-1}g)=g$. For $f=\sum_i c_i\underline b_i$ with $c_i\in R$ supplied by step 3, $B^{-1}(af)=(ac_i)_i$, so balancing and additivity give $\psi_U\mu_U(a\otimes f)=\sum_i ac_i\otimes\underline b_i=a\otimes\sum_i c_i\underline b_i=a\otimes f$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, so these identities prove that $\psi_U=\mu_U^{-1}$.

source.place: Pushing down by the trace: finite free constant lattice spanning the ambient vector space; explicit coordinate argument

proof.text: The coordinate tensor identification is $J:T\otimes_R R^r\to T^r$, $J(a\otimes(c_i))=(ac_i)_i$. Its inverse is $(t_i)\mapsto\sum_i t_i\otimes e_i$: $J$ of this sum is $(t_i)$, and the reverse composite sends $a\otimes(c_i)$ to $\sum_i ac_i\otimes e_i=a\otimes(c_i)$ by balancing. On these tensors the map $\mu_U$ after $1\otimes\phi_U$ equals $BJ$, so its matrix under the stated identification is exactly $B$. For $h:V\to U$, restriction on tensors sends $a\otimes f$ to $(a\circ|h|)\otimes(f\circ|h|)$ and on the target sends $g$ to $g\circ|h|$. Thus $\mu_V$ of the restricted tensor is $(af)\circ|h|$. Likewise $(B^{-1}(g\circ|h|))_i=(B^{-1}g)_i\circ|h|$, and the restrictions of $\underline b_i$ are the same constant sections. This proves restriction compatibility of both inverse maps.

source.place: Pushing down by the trace: finite free constant lattice spanning the ambient vector space; explicit coordinate argument

proof.text: The presheaf $K_S^r$ is a sheaf: glue each coordinate by the sheaf condition of $K_S$, and coordinatewise uniqueness proves uniqueness of the tuple. The natural inverse maps of steps 5–6 identify the sectionwise tensor presheaf with this sheaf. The sheaf tensor is its sheafification by [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product]. To see explicitly that sheafification changes nothing, write $P$ for this tensor presheaf and $\eta:P\to P^\#$ for its unit. Since $P$ is already a sheaf, the universal property in [def-weil-pbc-sheafification] gives $q:P^\#\to P$ with $q\eta=1_P$. Both $\eta q$ and $1_{P^\#}$ compose with $\eta$ to $\eta$, so uniqueness gives $\eta q=1_{P^\#}$. Consequently the sheafified $\mu$ is an isomorphism. On $a\otimes f$ its formula is $a\,\iota(f)$, so it is precisely the scalar extension of the actual inclusion, as asserted.

proof.text: When $r=0$, $K^0$, $A^0$ and $L$ are the zero module, each continuous-function module into them is zero, and all displayed sums are empty sums. The unique $0\times0$ matrix and its inverse act as the identity of the zero module. The tensor source is zero, since $a\otimes0=0$ and elementary tensors generate it. All inverse identities and restriction equalities above therefore also hold in rank zero.
